name: Audio and Video Evidence
title: Audio and Video Evidence
answer: Audio and video evidence in e-discovery covers the identification, preservation, processing, review, and production of sound recordings, voicemail, body camera footage, surveillance video, meeting recordings, and similar multimedia files that may be relevant to litigation or investigations. It extends beyond text search to include speech, speakers, scenes, objects, on-screen text, and metadata such as timestamps and device identifiers. The goal is to make these often large and unstructured files searchable and reviewable alongside email, chat, and documents.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Audio and video evidence in e-discovery covers the identification, preservation, processing, review, and production of sound recordings, voicemail, body camera footage, surveillance video, meeting recordings, and similar multimedia files that may be relevant to litigation or investigations. It extends beyond text search to include speech, speakers, scenes, objects, on-screen text, and metadata such as timestamps and device identifiers. The goal is to make these often large and unstructured files searchable and reviewable alongside email, chat, and documents.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Processing typically runs on cloud or on-premises servers with GPU acceleration for transcription, speaker separation, and object detection. Files are normalized into common formats and indexed so that review platforms can stream clips without downloading entire recordings. Storage and compute scale with the volume of footage, and many matters use dedicated media processing pipelines separate from standard document review databases.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by automated speech-to-text transcription, speaker diarization, scene and object recognition, and optical character recognition of text visible in video frames. Reviewers then search transcripts and detected entities, play back synchronized segments, and apply privilege or relevance tags. Quality control often involves human review of low-confidence transcriptions or disputed clips, and the output is produced with load files that link the media to its text and metadata.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on authentication, chain of custody, privacy, and the reliability of automated outputs. Courts may require a showing that a recording has not been altered and that any transcript or detection result is accurate enough to be used. Redaction of faces, voices, or bystander information raises proportionality and data protection concerns, and provenance records should document the original file, processing steps, and any manual corrections.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward faster, more accurate multimodal search that lets a reviewer query by spoken phrase, face, object, or action across millions of hours of footage. Generative summaries of long recordings and automated clip compilation are becoming more common, though their admissibility and explainability remain open questions. Expect tighter integration with review platforms and more attention to standards for authenticating machine-generated transcripts and detections.
